1.explanation: The gatherer response-compression.js inspects networkRecords and determines which resources were served without compression. Because it filters by MIME type and/or header detection, it isn’t recognizing gzip on application/json responses. The audit uses-request-compression.js then reads the gatherer’s results to flag uncompressed text resources. Fixing MIME detection or header checks in the gatherer (and, if necessary, adjusting the audit’s expectations in uses-request-compression.js) will resolve the false positive for gzipped JSON responses.
1.bug_scenario: When running Lighthouse’s “Enable text compression” audit against a JSON endpoint (/api/blob) served with gzip (Content-Encoding: gzip), the audit still reports /api/blob as uncompressed and lists large GZIP savings. A curl -I and Chrome’s Network panel both show compression is correctly applied, yet Lighthouse flags it as uncompressed.

2.explanation:
All of the compression-related logic lives in these three files:  
• response-compression.js is the gatherer that inspects networkRecords to detect and report which responses were compressed.  
• network-records.js is the computed artifact that normalizes DevTools Protocol resource timing and header fields (including transferSize/resourceSize and content-encoding) into the networkRecords that the gatherer consumes.  
• uses-request-compression.js is the audit that takes those records and flags any text-based resources that appear uncompressed.  
Because the gatherer/computed artifact isn’t picking up the gzip Content-Encoding header (or transferSize) correctly under this Chrome version, the audit always falls back to marking the resource as uncompressed. Fixing how networkRecords reads the Content-Encoding header or transferSize in network-records.js (and propagating that through response-compression.js into the audit) will resolve the false positives.
2.bug_scenario: When running Lighthouse (Chrome 63 dev) against an Express endpoint that responds with Content-Encoding: gzip, the “Enable text compression” (aka uses-text-compression / uses-response-compression) audit still flags every /api/blob response as uncompressed (~30 KB original, ~23 KB savings) even though curl -I and Chrome’s Network panel confirm gzip is applied.
